title: 1 Corinthians 9:24–27
context: Paul closes the chapter with images from the athletic games, which Corinth hosted every two years at the Isthmian festival. Runners compete for a perishable wreath, but believers run for an imperishable one, so they must exercise self-control. Paul disciplines his own body so that after preaching to others he himself will not be disqualified. Verse 27 is one of the classic passages in the debate over perseverance. Arminian readers often see a real possibility of final loss, while Reformed readers see a warning God uses to keep his people persevering, or read the disqualification as loss of reward rather than salvation.

verses.text: Don’t you know that those who run in a race all run, but one receives the prize? Run like that, that you may win.
verses.arminianNotes: All runners run, but only one receives the prize, so run to win. Arminian readers see a call to real effort in a race whose outcome is not automatic.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same call to effort. The point of the image is not that only one believer is saved but that each should run with the intensity of a competitor.

verses.text: Every man who strives in the games exercises self-control in all things. Now they do it to receive a corruptible crown, but we an incorruptible.
verses.arminianNotes: Every athlete exercises self-control to win a perishable wreath, but believers seek an imperishable one. Arminian readers see self-discipline as a necessary part of continuing in faith.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see self-control as a fruit of the Spirit and part of sanctification. The imperishable crown is sure for those God keeps, yet it is pursued through disciplined living.

verses.text: I therefore run like that, not aimlessly. I fight like that, not beating the air,
verses.arminianNotes: Paul does not run aimlessly or box as one beating the air. Arminian readers see purposeful, intentional discipleship that takes the goal seriously.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same purposefulness. Assurance of salvation does not make believers careless, but gives them a sure goal toward which to run.

verses.text: but I beat my body and bring it into submission, lest by any means, after I have preached to others, I myself should be rejected.
verses.arminianNotes: Paul disciplines his body and brings it into subjection, lest after preaching to others he himself should be disqualified. Arminian readers see a sober warning that even an apostle could finally fall away, and they take “disqualified” (adokimos) as rejection from the prize of salvation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers offer two main readings. Some, following Calvin, see disqualification as a real warning that God uses to keep his people faithful, since the elect persevere through such warnings, not apart from them. Others read it as losing reward or usefulness in ministry rather than salvation itself.
verses.keyContrast: Arminian readers see a real possibility that a believer, even a preacher, could be finally rejected. Reformed readers see either a means God uses to secure perseverance or a loss of reward and approval in ministry, not loss of salvation.
